summary: This informational document collects situations where wireless networks must behave with the reliability and predictability of wired ones, yet wires are not practical. Examples include aeronautical communications, amusement parks, industrial applications, pro audio and video, gaming, drone and vehicle control, edge robotics, and emergency vehicles. It supports the Reliable and Available Wireless work.

eli5.summary: Wires are dependable, but some things move around too much to use them. This is a list of jobs, like robots and rides, that need wireless that works every single time.

questions: reliable and available wireless use cases
subtitle: Wireless networks that deliver reliability like wired systems, for applications that cannot use cables

tldr.problem: Many critical applications need the reliability and low latency of wired networks, but wires are not practical for mobile devices, moving parts, or environments where installation costs are prohibitive.
tldr.mechanism: RAW (Reliable and Available Wireless) describes mechanisms to provide high reliability and availability for IP connectivity over wireless media by combining time synchronization, scheduling, redundant paths, and resource reservation.
tldr.outcome: Eight major application domains are identified where wireless reliability is essential: aviation, amusement parks, industrial control, professional audio and video, gaming, drones and vehicles, robotics, and emergency services.

today: RFC 9450 is an Informational RFC published in August 2023 that describes use cases motivating RAW technology development. The document itself is not obsoleted or updated. The use cases it describes inform ongoing standardization work in IETF working groups focused on time-sensitive and deterministic networking over wireless, including efforts to adapt DetNet mechanisms to wireless link-layer technologies.

sections.title: The Challenge of Reliable Wireless
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides protocols and mechanisms to deliver specified data streams with extremely low packet loss and bounded latency over wired networks using time synchronization, resource reservation, and traffic shaping. However, wireless transmission operates on a shared medium where signals interfere, fade, and are delayed unpredictably due to multipath propagation. Making wireless reliable and available is far more challenging than wiring, due to uncontrolled interference, self-induced multipath fading, and congestion losses on overbooked shared resources.

While open standards like Audio Video Bridging (AVB) and Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) focus on wired media, and DetNet has emphasized wired deployments, many critical applications fundamentally cannot use wires. Wireless is the only option for mobile or rotating devices, retrofitted buildings where running new cables is impractical, wearable sensors, autonomous vehicles, and immersive gaming. This document describes "RAW" (Reliable and Available Wireless)—mechanisms to achieve DetNet-like guarantees over wireless links—and enumerates the use cases that justify the extra technical effort required.
sections.eli5: Wires are safe because data moves predictably through them. Radio waves bounce around and get jammed easily, so making wireless as trustworthy as wires is very hard. But many things cannot be wired, so engineers need wireless that works reliably.

sections.title: Aeronautical and Aerospace Communications
sections.content:
Aircraft must maintain continuous, high-reliability communication with air-traffic control and airline operations throughout flight. Growing air traffic, especially in high-density regions like Europe and the US, is saturating the VHF frequency band used for voice communications, driving a transition to digital systems. The Future Communication Infrastructure for civil aviation includes satellite communications for oceanic regions, L-band Digital Aeronautical Communication System (LDACS) for air-to-ground and air-to-air communications, and AeroMACS for airport areas. These systems must support multiple priority levels of traffic: critical safety messages like collision warnings (TCAS) require ultra-low latency and near-perfect reliability, while routine communications can tolerate longer delays.

RAW requirements for aviation include bounded latency (30-90 ms forward, 60-120 ms return for LDACS), support for at least eight Classes of Service with different QoS requirements, and minimal protocol overhead since aeronautical links provide only kilobits per second of data rate. Modularity and interoperability across all 192 ICAO member nations is essential, as is the ability to handle high-speed mobile devices and maintain seamless handovers as aircraft move between coverage areas.
sections.eli5: Airplanes need to talk to people on the ground reliably while they are moving very fast. A broken wireless link could crash a plane, so every message must either get through or the pilot needs to know it failed.

sections.title: Industrial Control and Automation
sections.content:
Industrial processes rely on control loops where sensors measure physical properties (temperature, pressure, position), a programmable logic controller (PLC) makes decisions, and actuators perform actions (heat, move, stop). In process control industries like oil refining, loops typically run four times per second, while factory automation operates at millisecond timescales, and motion control may require sub-millisecond response times. A packet must flow from sensor to PLC to actuator within the loop period; even a rare loss of multiple packets in a row can halt production and cost the manufacturer dearly.

Wires were traditionally used for these control networks, but retrofitting older facilities built before the Internet age is expensive and time-consuming—deploying new cables can take months and cost tens of thousands of dollars. Furthermore, monitoring and diagnostics data must be handled separately from deterministic control flows for operational and security reasons. RAW enables deployment of a wireless network parallel to existing wired systems, carrying diagnostic telemetry and asynchronous data while preserving the reliability guarantees for critical control loops through scheduled access, time synchronization, and redundant paths.
sections.eli5: Factories have machines that listen to sensors and do what they are told: heat this, mix that, move here. If a wireless message is lost, the machine might break something. So wireless control must be as trustworthy as cables were.

sections.title: Professional Audio, Video, and Gaming
sections.content:
Professional audio and video delivery, live event production, augmented and virtual reality, and cloud gaming all require low and bounded latency because real-time delivery is essential for synchronized playback. In live audio to multiple speakers, latency must be consistent across feeds so sound stays synchronized with video. Professional audio systems stream over 802.11 wireless LAN, and gaming applications require sub-5-millisecond latency and less than 0.1 percent packet loss for responsive gameplay.

Wireless is the only practical option for many of these scenarios: deploying cables in historic buildings, large venues, or temporary event setups is impractical, and mobile devices demand wireless support. Buffering can compensate for some packet loss in streaming applications, but live applications cannot afford retransmission delays. Wireless networks supporting these uses must provide multipath capability for redundancy, traffic isolation to prevent congestion, and time-aware shaping to eliminate jitter and ensure bounded latency.
sections.eli5: Musicians and video people need wireless to work perfectly so that sound stays in sync with pictures and games respond instantly to button presses. If the wireless link hiccups, the show looks broken.

sections.title: Unmanned Systems and Autonomous Vehicles
sections.content:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (drones), autonomous cars, and vehicle platoons require continuous reliable communication with control centers and with each other. Remote maneuvering of a drone may occur over cellular networks, but situations requiring very low latency and deterministic behavior—such as drone-to-drone platooning or offloading computation to a neighboring drone—need wireless RAW mechanisms. Similarly, autonomous vehicles traveling in platoons with reduced spacing to improve highway efficiency require ultra-reliable, low-latency links to transmit commands and safety-critical information among vehicles.

These systems use diverse wireless technologies (cellular, IEEE 802.11, 802.15.4 TSCH) and must self-configure without manual setup, support heterogeneous traffic types from ultra-critical to best-effort, and handle mobility gracefully. When services are decomposed into functions distributed across multiple vehicles or edge devices and chained together, each link must guarantee specific requirements for latency, bandwidth, and jitter.
sections.eli5: Robots and drones flying together need to tell each other what to do without delay or error. A broken wireless link could cause a crash or a collision, so every message matters.

sections.title: Edge Robotics and Emergency Services
sections.content:
Robots deployed in shared environments like shopping malls or warehouse pickup points offload computation to network edge devices rather than running everything locally, enabling centralized coordination of multiple robots performing complex tasks like search and rescue, goods delivery, or cleaning. Robot control requires very low latency (0.5 to 20 milliseconds) between the robot and the edge controller. Instrumented emergency vehicles (ambulances) transmit vital signs data from patients, position data to dispatchers, and coordination information between first responders, all through radio systems in urban or rural environments, possibly during natural disasters when infrastructure is damaged.

Both scenarios demand high availability and rapid recovery from link failures, heterogeneous traffic types with different priorities, and end-to-end security for sensitive data. Emergency systems must also operate in degraded states and support rapid handover when moving between coverage areas. RAW mechanisms that employ redundant paths (called "Tracks" in the specification) and dynamic rerouting enable these systems to maintain connectivity even when individual wireless links fail.
sections.eli5: Robots in shopping malls and ambulance crews need wireless that never breaks down, because if it does, someone might not get help. In emergencies, the network itself might be damaged, so the system needs backup paths.
